headline: Youth unemployment rose to 12.4% in 2025
detail: 67 million young people unemployed; NEET share rose to 20%, more than 257 million people.
comparator: Youth unemployment rose in 8 of 11 subregions between 2023 and 2025.
caveat: Establishes youth labour-market strain, not an AI effect.
why: Sets the baseline: AI is entering a youth labour market already under pressure.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
headline: Recent graduate unemployment about 5.6%; underemployment 42%
detail: Recent college graduates remained in a difficult labour market through Q2 2026.
comparator: Underemployment remains elevated and unemployment is high for a group normally advantaged by higher education.
why: Shows pressure at the graduate transition point independently of AI exposure measures.

headline: Graduate postings about 7% lower year on year
detail: Overall UK postings were 11% below the start of 2026 and 32% below the February 2020 baseline; summer jobs were at a four-year low.
comparator: AI appeared in a record 9.4% of UK postings while graduate and summer hiring remained weak.
caveat: Graduate series is based on postings explicitly labelled graduate; co-movement does not prove AI causality.
why: Captures contraction and technological transition occurring at the same time.

headline: Junior-level postings fell 7% during 2025
detail: Senior-level postings rose 4% over the same period, while recent-graduate jobseeker activity increased sharply.
comparator: Junior and senior hiring moved in opposite directions.
caveat: Platform vacancy data cover only part of total hiring.
why: Shows experience-level divergence in US demand.

headline: Vacancies fell to 707,000; unemployment 4.9%
detail: Payrolled employment in June 2026 was 78,000 lower than a year earlier.
comparator: Vacancies were at a level last recorded outside the pandemic in 2014.
why: Important competing context: employer caution is economy-wide.

source: Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development
headline: 62% of employers planned to recruit in the next three months
detail: Private-sector recruitment intentions were 57%, the lowest since the measure began in 2016 outside the pandemic.
comparator: Private-sector hiring intent remains unusually weak.
caveat: Intentions, not realized hires; not youth-specific.
why: Supports a broad cyclical explanation that must be separated from entry-level effects.

headline: 22–25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations show a 19% relative employment gap
detail: The gap widened through June 2026 and appears mainly through reduced hiring rather than increased separations.
comparator: Experienced workers and less-exposed young workers do not show the same pattern.
caveat: Descriptive rather than causal; ADP effects are stronger than some national benchmarks and some divergence predates genAI.
why: The strongest age × exposure signal in the evidence base.

headline: Monthly listings fell about 20% in highly exposed and highly substitutable white-collar occupations
detail: Relative declines were largest in business services, IT, entry-level and upper-middle-skilled work.
caveat: Online vacancies are concentrated in parts of the South Asian white-collar market and are not the whole labour market.
why: Independent geography and design with a similar exposure × substitutability pattern.

headline: 37% of young workers globally are in medium-to-high AI-exposure occupations
detail: Exposure rises to 69% in Northern America and 63% in Europe; the report states that entry-level hiring slowdowns are evident while AI's role remains contested.
comparator: The report notes that some entry-level vacancy weakness began before ChatGPT.
caveat: Synthesis draws partly on other data streams and should not be counted as an independent causal test.
why: Provides a deliberately cautious institutional framing close to the paper's own conclusion.

headline: Entry-level hiring underperformed overall hiring by only 0.4–2.0 points across five markets
detail: Within AI-augmented occupations, junior hiring ran 3–10 percentage points below hiring in those occupations overall.
comparator: Broad entry-level slowdown looks mostly cyclical; occupational and experience-level composition remains suggestive.
caveat: LinkedIn membership and profile updates are not representative of whole labour markets.
why: A strong counter-signal against a simplistic AI-collapse narrative while retaining an AI-shaped composition effect.

headline: One-third of surveyed employers reported replacing at least some entry-level jobs with AI
detail: Technology and manufacturing were among the most prominent sectors; coding, data entry and customer-service work were frequently mentioned.
comparator: Employer confidence in graduate management education remained high at the same time.
caveat: Survey is focused on employers engaged with graduate management talent and is not representative of all employers.
why: Direct employer-reported evidence that some substitution has moved from expectation to practice.

headline: 87% expect AI to reshape graduate and apprentice roles
detail: 43% said entry-level roles had already evolved without formal redesign; 40% expected no replacement, 42% expected 1–10%, and 18% expected larger-scale replacement.
comparator: Task and role change is broader than headcount replacement.
caveat: Employer survey; expectations are not realized economy-wide effects.
why: Important counterweight: redesign is widespread, wholesale replacement is not.

source: National Association of Colleges and Employers
headline: 43% of graduating bachelor's students had at least one job offer before graduation
detail: Average offers were 0.79; outcomes were similar to 2025 but materially weaker than 2022 and 2023.
caveat: Student survey and graduate-specific, not economy-wide and not AI-specific.
why: Entrant-side evidence of a tougher transition and the value of real workplace experience.

headline: 35% believed AI had reduced their career opportunities
detail: 16% believed AI had increased opportunities; 41% were not very or not at all confident they were developing the AI-related skills they needed.
comparator: Finding suitable opportunities, competition and insufficient experience were major barriers.
caveat: Perception evidence can move ahead of realized employment effects.
why: Shows that young people themselves see opportunity and capability pressure.

headline: 68% see AI skills as essential; only 48% say staff help them develop those skills
comparator: A 20-point gap between perceived need and perceived institutional support.
caveat: Education perception survey, not an employment outcome measure.
why: Connects changing workplace capability expectations to the education-to-work transition.

headline: 1.67 million active postings in July, up 7.7% year on year
detail: Hospitality, tourism and construction showed strong growth; REC cautioned that many entry-level opportunities had not recovered to the same extent.
comparator: Provides a recovery signal against the earlier 2026 downturn.
caveat: Aggregate recovery does not establish entry-level recovery.
why: Crucial falsification monitor: if junior hiring recovers with the wider market, cyclical explanations gain weight.

headline: Permanent placements stabilized after 45 consecutive months of decline
detail: Temporary vacancies increased for the first time in two years and overall demand fell at its softest rate in 22 months.
comparator: Early sign that the broader market may be stabilizing.
caveat: Does not isolate graduate or youth hiring.
why: Supports the site's relative-recovery test rather than a one-way deterioration narrative.

headline: Technology shocks can appear through weaker opportunities for newcomers rather than visible incumbent layoffs
detail: The OECD Employment Outlook highlights adjustment through joblessness and changing opportunities available to new entrants.
comparator: Explains why aggregate employment can look resilient while entry routes deteriorate.
caveat: Conceptual mechanism, not a direct estimate of the current AI effect on youth hiring.
why: Supports monitoring hiring and entry rather than waiting for mass layoffs.
